summary:
Lunaris is a web tool for mission planners, educators and the public that compares lunar south pole landing sites and dates in seconds. Near the pole the Sun stays a few degrees above the skyline, so a distant hill or a one-week launch slip can cost a mission its power or its link to Earth.

For five curated sites or any clicked point between 60°S and the pole, Lunaris shows the Sun and the Earth against the real terrain horizon from NASA LOLA topography, with solar elevation, time to sunset and Earthset, and Deep Space Network visibility. It scores each mission from 0 to 100 for power, communication and slope, compares two scenarios side by side, shows what a date slip does, and suggests a better landing date or a better spot within 500 m. Mission limits are adjustable and every scenario can be shared as a link. A 3D view on real LOLA terrain and an Explorer mode with a guided tour and a landing game bring the same results to students.

Sun and Earth positions come from JPL DE421 and match JPL Horizons within 0.00002°. A backtest on Chandrayaan-3 places its real landing date inside the predicted low-risk window.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunaris answers one question for the lunar south pole: "if the landing date or the landing spot changes, does the mission still have power and a link to Earth?"

- Planner: five curated sites (Shackleton crater, Shackleton–de Gerlache ridge, Mons Mouton / IM-2, Malapert A / IM-1, Chandrayaan-3) plus Apollo 11 as an equatorial reference, or any clicked point between 60°S and the pole. For each one: a horizon panorama from LOLA terrain with the Sun and the Earth, solar elevation, time to sunset and Earthset, visible share of the solar disk, and which DSN complex sees the Moon.

- Side-by-side comparison of two scenarios (site, date, or both), a "slip" control, and a timeline animation.

- A transparent risk score: power (longest darkness vs battery, usable Sun), communication (longest outage, daily contact), and surface (95th-percentile slope within the landing precision), each 0–100, with a plain-language verdict and a re-check against the LOLA map's height error.

- Alternatives: a landing-date strip that colours every date up to 2030 by risk, plus suggestions for a better date and a better spot within ±500 m (an 81-point grid shown as a heat map).

- Mission profiles (generic, solar lander, battery rover based on NASA's VIPER figures) and sliders for every limit. Every scenario can be shared as a URL.

- 3D surface view on real LOLA terrain with GPU shadows, the Sun's and the Earth's tracks over the mission, and a drone view with a lander at true size.

- Explorer mode for students and the public: an introduction, a guided tour with live cards (is the Sun up, how long the battery lasts, which antenna is listening), and a landing game with three missions.

HOW IT WORKS

Python with Skyfield and JPL DE421 computes hourly Sun and Earth vectors in the Moon's mean-Earth frame. Libration and disk sizes are included, and there is no atmosphere, so no refraction. The terrain horizon covers 720 directions out to 250 km on NASA LOLA 60 m topography and includes lunar curvature. The risk model was written in Python and ported to TypeScript, so all scoring runs in the browser, and a validation script checks that both give identical results. A FastAPI service on Google Cloud Run computes the horizon of any clicked point by reading the LOLA GeoTIFFs with HTTP requests.

VALIDATION

- Skyfield vs JPL Horizons: at most 0.00002° difference.

- Rise and set times vs one-minute Horizons tables: median 0.0 min on the sphere model.

- Malapert A ground height matches IM-1's landing elevation.

- Backtest on Chandrayaan-3 (landed 2023-08-23): the real date scores risk 0 and lies inside the model's low-risk window (21–24 Aug), and the model's sunset matches the day ISRO put the lander to sleep.

TOOLS

Python (Skyfield, NumPy, rasterio, FastAPI), TypeScript, React, Vite, Leaflet with NASA Moon Trek tiles, three.js, Radix UI, Google Cloud Run, Vercel.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Mission planners can screen dates and sites in seconds instead of juggling Horizons, QuickMap and raw tables. Educators and the public can see why the lunar south pole is both attractive and hard. Every limit is visible and adjustable, and every number comes from NASA/JPL data, not from a black box.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

One site-independent vector table lets the browser analyse any point on the Moon. The "slip" view turns launch delays into an immediate visual answer. The same horizon computation drives both the numbers and the 3D view, so what you see is what is scored.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy against authoritative sources, honest limits (the risk thresholds are assumptions and can be changed; the score is a comparison heuristic, not a flight-safety metric), speed, phone use, and keeping the site usable if the terrain service is down.
